step4.objective:
• An ICMP Echo Reply returned for each unicast Echo Request addressed to the device, with identifier, sequence number and payload unchanged.
  • The Echo Reply source address identical to the destination address of the corresponding Echo Request, on every interface that holds an address.
  • On an interface with multiple addresses, each reply sourced from the specific address that the matching request was sent to.
  • Replies sourced from the requested address even when the reply leaves through a different interface from the one owning that address.
  • The Echo Reply source address following the requested address in a virtualised management-fabric node as on a physical device.
  • No Echo Reply sent for a request addressed to an address the device does not own, and no reply sourced from an unrelated local address.
  • Correct reply source selection maintained across address changes, with replies sourced only from addresses currently configured.

steps.description: Note: Related ART Tests linked in Traceability.

Verify Echo Reply generation for unicast Echo Requests sent from a test endpoint to an address configured on the DUT, using a range of payload sizes and patterns. Confirm a reply is returned for each request and that the identifier, sequence number and payload in each reply match the corresponding request.

Configure an address on every DUT interface type that can hold one (e.g. switch ports, VLAN interfaces, loopback and management interfaces). Send Echo Requests to each address in turn and capture the replies. Confirm that the source address of each reply matches the destination address of its request.

Configure multiple addresses on a single DUT interface, including both primary and secondary addresses. Send interleaved Echo Requests to each of those addresses from the same test endpoint. Confirm that each reply is sourced from the specific address the matching request targeted, not from the interface's primary address.

Using a topology with at least two links between the DUT and its partner, send Echo Requests to an address owned by one DUT interface, with routing arranged so that the reply leaves through a different interface. Repeat with a loopback address as the target. Confirm that the replies are sourced from the requested address and not from the egress interface's address.

Repeat the single-address, multi-address and asymmetric-path scenarios against a virtualised management-fabric node hosted within the fabric, targeting its fabric and non-fabric addresses. Confirm that the reply source address behaves the same as it does on a physical device.

Send Echo Requests to an address in a DUT-connected subnet that no device owns, and to an address that belongs to a different device. Confirm that the DUT sends no Echo Reply for these requests and does not answer from any of its own local addresses.

While continuous Echo Requests are being sent to DUT addresses, add a new address, remove an existing address and change an address on an interface. Confirm that requests to the new address get replies sourced from it, that requests to a removed or replaced address get no reply, and that the remaining addresses keep sourcing their replies correctly.

Bring an addressed interface down and back up, then restart the DUT with the address configuration saved. Send Echo Requests to each configured address again. Confirm that the reply source still matches the request destination and that no reply uses a stale address.

You are drafting Zephyr-ready verification steps for a manual test case. The objective below is finalized (user-reviewed). Derive the steps from it. An objective bullet states an END STATE — what should be true. A step is a PROCEDURE — what someone does, and under what conditions. A step must add test-design information the bullet does not already carry: the setup, the data, the variation, the thing being exercised. Re-wording a bullet adds nothing and is not a step — whatever verb it opens with. "Verify …" is a perfectly good way to begin a real step and many steps here should use it; the fault is restatement, never the word. ## Case AWPTCM-T33242 — ICMP echo reply (ICMP suite) ## Finalized objective (authoritative)
  • An ICMP Echo Reply returned for each unicast Echo Request addressed to the device, with identifier, sequence number and payload unchanged.
  • The Echo Reply source address identical to the destination address of the corresponding Echo Request, on every interface that holds an address.
  • On an interface with multiple addresses, each reply sourced from the specific address that the matching request was sent to.
  • Replies sourced from the requested address even when the reply leaves through a different interface from the one owning that address.
  • The Echo Reply source address following the requested address in a virtualised management-fabric node as on a physical device.
  • No Echo Reply sent for a request addressed to an address the device does not own, and no reply sourced from an unrelated local address.
  • Correct reply source selection maintained across address changes, with replies sourced only from addresses currently configured.
## TestLink selections (evidence — reuse their concrete values where they fit) - AWP-9996: The IP source address in an ICMP Echo Reply - AWP-21047: ATMF VM : The IP source address in an ICMP Echo Reply ## Zephyr exemplars (evidence — match their level of detail) - AWPTCM-T2068: ATMF VM : The IP source address in an ICMP Echo Reply - AWPTCM-T7540: The IP source address in an ICMP Echo Reply ## ATPyLib coverage (selected ART) - 2010.3.2: The IP source address in an ICMP Echo Reply MUST be the same as the specific-destination address of the corresponding ICMP Echo Request - 2002.3.2: The IP source address in an ICMP Echo Reply MUST be the same as thespecific-destination address of the corresponding ICMP Echo Request - 2005.10.1: The source address of an Echo Reply sent in response to a unicast Echo Request message MUST be the same as the destination address of that Echo Request message ## Rules - The FIRST step is injected server-side as a traceability note — DO NOT generate it. - Generate ONLY the subsequent verification steps exercising the objective's artefacts. - Cover each major objective bullet: positive, negative, special conditions, reporting. - Keep each step high-level enough to be reusable across platforms, but specific enough to be testable. Naming exact values, counts and timings is the PyTest script's job, not this one — a manual step that dictates them narrows the tester to one way of exercising the feature instead of leaving them to produce evidence that it works. - LEAVE `expectedResult` EMPTY on every step. This is deliberate, not an omission. The tester reads the objective and the step and reasons out what should happen; stating the outcome narrows them to producing exactly that result instead of evidence that the feature works. The objective already carries the expected outcomes. - Say WHAT is being exercised, not which command to type. Proving the step was taken — capturing `show` output as evidence — is the generated PyTest script's job, and naming commands or device registers here invents mechanisms that may not exist and narrows the tester besides. - Where a step depends on topology, say which roles it needs (e.g. two links between the DUT and a partner), never a device model or a port number. - Platform-agnostic language: no product names, no hardcoded port strings. ## Output format — this example IS the specification; match its level of detail [ { "description": "Verify LLDP operation with the DUT and its link partner both running default timers. Confirm neighbours are discovered on the test link and that each side reports the other's chassis and port identity.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Vary the transmit interval and hold multiplier across their supported range, including the minimum and maximum. Confirm advertisements are sent at the configured rate and that the neighbour's advertised lifetime tracks the configured values.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Set the transmit interval below the supported minimum and above the supported maximum. Confirm the DUT rejects both and retains its previous configuration.", "expectedResult": "" }, { "description": "Disable LLDP transmit on the DUT while leaving receive enabled, then re-enable it. Confirm the neighbour ages out and is rediscovered, and that the port reports the change.", "expectedResult": "" } ] Output the JSON array ONLY. No prose, no markdown fence.

• An ICMP Echo Reply returned for each unicast Echo Request addressed to the device, with identifier, sequence number and payload unchanged.
  • The Echo Reply source address identical to the destination address of the corresponding Echo Request, on every interface that holds an address.
  • On an interface with multiple addresses, each reply sourced from the specific address that the matching request was sent to.
  • Replies sourced from the requested address even when the reply leaves through a different interface from the one owning that address.
  • The Echo Reply source address following the requested address in a virtualised management-fabric node as on a physical device.
  • No Echo Reply sent for a request addressed to an address the device does not own, and no reply sourced from an unrelated local address.
  • Correct reply source selection maintained across address changes, with replies sourced only from addresses currently configured.

gaps: The selected ART coverage (2010.3.2, 2002.3.2, 2005.10.1) reasonably addresses the core RFC conformance behaviour: the source address of an ICMP Echo Reply matches the specific destination address of the corresponding unicast Echo Request, for both ICMPv4 and ICMPv6. The coverage is less clear on device-specific context from the TestLink and Zephyr artefacts, namely replies sourced from an address configured on the default VLAN1 interface rather than a generic test interface. Dual-stack validation on the same interface, as called out in AWP-21047, also lacks explicit coverage. The ATMF VM variant (AWP-21047 / AWPTCM-T2068) has no evident automated counterpart, so behaviour on virtualised ATMF platforms remains unverified. Edge conditions are also not clearly exercised, including multiple or secondary addresses on the same interface, replies when the destination is a non-primary address, and any interaction with management or VRF contexts.
